The Dwarf Mini is compact. So portable, in fact, that it's as small as a carton of chocolate milk. Jamie Carter The Dwarflab Mini is portable enough that you can take it anywhere. Jamie Carter Jamie Carter Jamie Carter The Dwarf Mini's power lies in its extremely small form factor. Despite its size, it is still more than capable of capturing detailed astrophotography, even in light-polluted areas. This makes it suitable for those who live in cities as well as those who like to travel to dark sky sites for their stargazing sessions.

It is easy to use and, once set up, automatically finds and tracks targets while the image of your chosen nebula or star cluster appears on your smartphone screen. Despite being perfect for beginners who want easy shots of the night sky, it can be suitable for those who are more experienced in astronomy as a portable astro option.

The full moon, as imaged by the Dwarflab Dwarf Mini. Jamie Carter The Beehive Cluster, as imaged by the Dwarflab Dwarf Mini. Jamie Carter If you don't want to carry around lots of heavy gear, this is a great lightweight option for quick shots of the night sky or the moon. It's perfect for throwing into a backpack and chasing eclipses, weighing only 1.8 lbs (840 g) and featuring a built-in solar filter. It also includes a mosaic mode that means you can capture a larger portion of the sky without having to stitch together separate frames.

This is a great Black Friday deal but we would still recommend this at full price thanks to its easy operation and ideal travel size. Reviews consensus: In our Dwarflab Dwarf Mini review , expert Jamie said it "makes capturing the deep sky and the solar system almost effortless," awarding it four stars. He did note that its 2MP sensor means the images it produces are best suited to sharing on smartphones.

Space: ★★★★ | T3: ★★★★ | LiveScience: ★★★★

✅ Buy it if: You want a smart telescope you can take anywhere without worrying about heavy kit weighing you down.

❌ Don't buy it if: You want to show your images off on bigger screens. A smart telescope with higher resolution would be better instead, like the ZWO Seestar S50 Pro.
